main_body: Flat ground patch: a brick/paving floor of beige and pink-grey stones in running bond with dark grey mortar joints, plus a few blue-grey patches and grey/white strips with dark bars along some rows. It is a terrain tile surface, not a standing object.
top_band: none - ground paving is a flat surface seen from above; there is no standing body to read a top band and front face from
evidence: The candidate is a flat paving patch of terrain, so the standing-object 3/4 contract does not really apply. The brick pattern reads as a floor surface or wall face, with no top/front structure to judge. Nothing in it fails the contract in the sense of a standing object drawn wrongly, but strictly there is no 3/4 construction either. The dark-green bars with grey/white strips at the top right and mid-right look like stray edge fragments of a wall or cliff face rather than a clear 3/4 construction. Since the kind is terrain, I treat the lack of a top/front split as not applicable, but being strict, the stray fragments make it ambiguous.

style.evidence: Compared with the references (grass with tufts and dark clumps, cobble paving with per-stone shading), the candidate is a regular brick pattern with about 4 lightness steps: beige, light pink-grey, mid grey-brown and dark grey mortar. Mortar lines are a neutral dark grey rather than a tinted dark material tone, so the outline is mixed. Several bricks have 5x3 or larger blocks of a single flat beige, and the repeating pattern looks mechanical, with little per-stone grain or highlight/shadow variation. The blue-grey patches and the grey/white strips with dark green bars look unrelated to the brick and add inconsistency rather than richness. Density per tile is lower than the cobble reference, which shades every stone individually. A careful artist would see it as thinner and flatter than the reference.
